When did Jesus say the kingdom would be taken from the leaders and given to others (Matthew 21:43-45)?
In their own time. The chief priests and Pharisees knew he was speaking about them, so the transfer was not two thousand years away.

After the parable of the tenants, Jesus said, "The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits" (Matthew 21:43). Matthew adds that the chief priests and Pharisees "perceived that he was speaking about them" (Matthew 21:45). The parable ends with the owner coming and destroying the tenants (Matthew 21:40-41). The next parable has a king who sends troops and burns the city of those who refused his wedding feast (Matthew 22:7). On the covenantal reading, these scenes point to AD 70. The "people producing fruit" is the church of believing Jews and Gentiles (1 Peter 2:9). The stone that crushes (Matthew 21:44) echoes Daniel 2:34-35, where the kingdom stone breaks the old powers.
Matthew 22:7: "The king was angry. He sent his armies, destroyed those murderers and burned their city." Jerusalem burned in AD 70.
1 Peter 2:9 gives the church Israel's titles from Exodus 19:6: a royal priesthood and a holy nation.

Most interpreters agree the parable targets the leaders of that day. Dispensationalists say the kingdom is taken from that generation of leaders, not from Israel forever, and will be restored at Christ's return (Acts 1:6-7; Romans 11). Covenant theologians say the true Israel continues in the church with its Jewish remnant.
Does "this generation" mean any people, in any age, who share the same evil traits?
This reading says no. Jesus tied the judgment to a specific group he was addressing, and the leaders understood he meant them.

Some writers, such as Dave Hunt, have suggested that anyone at any time with the same evil tendencies would belong to that "generation of vipers". The fulfilled reading answers that this makes the phrase timeless and almost empty. Jesus said, "All these things will come upon this generation" (Matthew 23:36). He then said, "This generation will not pass away until all these things take place" (Matthew 24:34). A time limit does not make sense if the group never ends. There is also a moral risk. Making the phrase timeless can turn a judgment on one generation into a charge against Jewish people in every age. That is not what the text says. Christians in every age are warned from the passage, but the prophecy itself was aimed at one generation.
Matthew 23:36 and 24:34 both begin "Truly I say to you": a solemn statement to the listeners in front of him.
Acts 2:40: Peter urged his hearers, "Save yourselves from this crooked generation." He meant people then alive.

Some scholars hold that "generation" (genea) can carry a moral sense, "this kind of people", as in Psalms 12:7 or Philippians 2:15. On that view the evil kind lasts until Christ returns. Others answer that even the moral sense in the Gospels is always applied to people living at the time.
How do Matthew 23:36 and 24:34 work together?
They act like bookends. Both say "this generation" and both start with "Truly I say to you". The events between them fall within that time frame.

Matthew 23:36 says, "Truly, all these things will come upon this generation." Matthew 24:34 says, "Truly, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place." The disciples' questions in 24:3 were raised by what Jesus had just said in chapter 23. So the two chapters belong together. On the fulfilled reading, the two time statements frame the signs that sit between them. If 23:36 means Jesus' contemporaries, and nearly everyone agrees it does, then 24:34 should mean the same people. To change the meaning in the second verse, a reader needs a clear signal in the text. This reading finds none. The Old Covenant order would end with the fall of the temple, which was the sign of the "end of the age".
The parallel accounts keep the same frame: Mark 13:30 and Luke 21:32 repeat the generation statement.
Luke 11:50-51 says the blood of the prophets "will be required of this generation", using the same idea as Matthew 23:36.

Many scholars accept the link but see two answers in the discourse. On this view Matthew 24:4-35 covers AD 70 and 24:36-25:46 covers the final return ("that day"). Dispensationalists usually take "all these things" in 24:34 to mean the end-time signs, so "this generation" is the one that sees them.
How is the phrase "this generation" used elsewhere in the Gospels?
In every other Gospel use it means the people alive when Jesus spoke. The fulfilled reading asks why Matthew 24:34 should be the single exception.

The phrase appears more than a dozen times in the Gospels. Jesus compares "this generation" to children in the market (Matthew 11:16; Luke 7:31). He says no sign will be given to "this generation" except Jonah (Matthew 12:39-41; Mark 8:12; Luke 11:29-30). The Queen of the South will condemn it (Luke 11:31). The blood of the prophets will be charged to it (Luke 11:50-51). The Son of Man must be rejected by it (Luke 17:25). In each case the meaning is plain: the people living then. On this reading, the rule is simple. Let Scripture interpret Scripture. When a phrase has one steady meaning in all its uses, the reader should not give it a new meaning in one verse to fit a system.
Luke 17:25: "He must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation." That happened in AD 30 or 33, not in a future age.
Mark 8:12: "Why does this generation seek a sign?" was said to Pharisees standing in front of him.

Some futurists answer that context can change a word's meaning. They argue that the signs in Matthew 24 never happened in full in the first century, so the phrase must mean a later generation. Others accept the normal meaning and say "all these things" refers only to the events before the coming, not the coming itself.
Why does it matter that Jesus said "this" generation and not "that" generation?
"This" points to what is near, "that" to what is far. Matthew uses "that day" for distant time. Jesus chose "this" for the generation listening.

In Greek, as in English, "this" (houtos) points to something present or near. "That" (ekeinos) points to something more distant. Matthew uses both carefully. He writes "to this day" for his own time (Matthew 27:8; 28:15). He uses "on that day" for the future judgment (Matthew 7:22) and "that day and hour" for the unknown time (Matthew 24:36). If Jesus had meant a far-off group, he could have said, "That generation will not pass away." On the fulfilled reading, the choice of "this" is a deliberate signal. It ties the prophecy to the people who heard it. The change from "this" in verse 34 to "that day" in verse 36 is one reason some see a shift of subject there.
Matthew 27:8: the potter's field is called the Field of Blood "to this day", meaning Matthew's own time.
Matthew 24:36: "concerning that day and hour no one knows"; the far demonstrative appears right after verse 34.

Futurist scholars reply that "this" can point to the generation just described in the text, the one that "sees all these things" (Matthew 24:33). They say the demonstrative refers back to the signs, not to the listeners. Others answer that verse 33 itself says "you" will see them.
What does the repeated word "you" in the Olivet Discourse tell us?
It shows Jesus was speaking to his disciples about their own future. "You will hear", "they will deliver you", "when you see" all point to the listeners.

In the discourse Jesus says: "See that no one leads you astray" (Matthew 24:4). "You will hear of wars" (24:6). "They will deliver you up and kill you" (24:9). "When you see the abomination" (24:15). "Pray that your flight may not be in winter" (24:20). "When you see all these things" (24:33). Luke adds that they would be brought before kings and governors (Luke 21:12-13). On the fulfilled reading, a listener on the Mount of Olives would conclude that these events would happen in his lifetime. If Jesus meant a far future, we would expect "when they see" and "they will deliver them". The book of Acts then shows these very things happening to the same disciples. The plain sense of "you" agrees with the plain sense of "this generation".
Acts 4:3 and 5:40: Peter and John are arrested and flogged, as Matthew 10:17 and 24:9 foretold.
Acts 25:23: Paul stands before King Agrippa and Governor Festus, as Luke 21:12 foretold.

Futurists answer that the disciples stand for later believers, or for the Jewish remnant of the end time. They note that prophets often addressed people as though they would see events that came later. Moderate readers say the "you" fits AD 70 in the first part and believers in all ages in the second part.
Does "Zechariah, whom you murdered" (Matthew 23:35) prove that "you" can mean people long dead?
This reading says no. Jesus treats the living generation as sharing their fathers' guilt, and says the judgment will fall on them. The "you" still means his listeners.

Some futurists, such as Stanley Toussaint, argue that since Zechariah died centuries earlier, "you" in Matthew 24 can also mean people who are not contemporaries. The fulfilled reading answers in three steps. First, Jesus addresses the living leaders. They are "filling up" their fathers' measure (Matthew 23:32). They are one with their fathers in guilt, as they themselves admit by building the prophets' tombs (Matthew 23:29-31). Second, Jesus says the penalty "will come upon this generation" (23:36). The punishment falls on the living, not on the dead. Third, "may" is not "must". Showing that "you" can stretch in one special case does not prove it stretches in the discourse. The burden of proof lies with the reader who changes the plain meaning. The text names the living as the ones judged.
Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:20-22). He is the last martyr in the Hebrew Bible's order, as Abel is the first.
Nehemiah 9:33-34 shows a later generation confessing "we have acted wickedly" for their fathers' sins: shared corporate guilt.

Futurists hold that the corporate "you" shows a prophet can speak to a nation across time. On that view the disciples in Matthew 24 represent the faithful of the end time. Scholars debate whether Zechariah son of Barachiah is the priest of 2 Chronicles 24, the prophet Zechariah, or someone else.
How did earlier Bible commentators read "this generation" in Matthew 24:34?
Many saw it as Jesus' own generation, with fulfillment in the fall of Jerusalem. This view was common long before modern dispensationalism.

A range of respected commentators read the phrase as Jesus' contemporaries. John Lightfoot (1658) said the verses before 24:34 speak of Jerusalem's ruin and that John and some rabbis lived to see it. Thomas Newton (1754) wondered how anyone could split the discourse when verse 34 is so plain. John Gill (1746-48) saw it as full proof that the whole section concerns the end of the Jewish state. In modern times D. A. Carson and William Lane said the phrase can only with great difficulty mean anything else, and R. T. France agreed. On this reading, the agreement of these careful scholars shows that the first-century view is not a new or fringe idea. Many of them still believed in a future bodily return of Christ.
Eusebius (Church History 3.5-3.8, about AD 325) described the fall of Jerusalem as fulfilling Jesus' prophecy, quoting Josephus at length.
John Calvin, on Matthew 24:34, said Jesus meant the destruction of the city would come within the lifetime of his hearers.

Several of these scholars, including Carson, still read Matthew 24:36 onward as the final return. Dispensational writers point to other commentators, such as some church fathers, who read the discourse as about the end of the world. They note that a majority view does not settle meaning.
Does Matthew 23:39, "You will not see me until you say, Blessed is he who comes", promise a future national conversion of Israel?
On this reading, "until" states a condition, not a promise. They will see him as Savior only when they welcome him. It does not say when, or that all will.

Some futurists read Matthew 23:39 as a promise that Israel as a nation will one day repent. The fulfilled reading notes that the verse begins with "for", linking it to the abandoned house in 23:38. R. T. France points out that the Greek expresses a possibility, not a firm prediction. Matthew often uses "until" in this conditional way. "You will not get out until you pay the last penny" (Matthew 5:26). The servant was jailed "until he should pay" (Matthew 18:30, 34). Men vowed not to eat "until they had killed Paul", and that never happened (Acts 23:12). In the years after Pentecost thousands of Jewish people did confess Jesus as the one who comes in the Lord's name (Acts 2:41; 4:4). The door was open. Those who refused faced him as judge.
Acts 3:19-21: Peter urged Jerusalem to repent "so that times of refreshing may come": a conditional offer.
Psalms 118:26 is the source of "Blessed is he who comes"; the crowds used it at the triumphal entry (Matthew 21:9).

Many scholars, both futurist and non-futurist, see hope in this verse. They link it with Romans 11:25-26 and Zechariah 12:10, expecting a large turning of Jewish people to Christ before his return. Postmillennialists and some amillennialists also expect such a turning, while denying a rebuilt temple.
Was there still hope for Jewish people after Jesus declared the temple desolate?
Yes. The gospel went "to the Jew first", and thousands believed. The hope was in Christ and his new temple, the church, not in a restored building.

Jesus' sentence on the temple was not a sentence on every Jewish person. Peter preached in Jerusalem, and about three thousand believed in one day (Acts 2:41). Soon the men alone numbered about five thousand (Acts 4:4). Later James told Paul that "many thousands" of Jewish believers lived in Judea (Acts 21:20). Paul himself was a Jewish believer and called himself proof that God had not rejected his people (Romans 11:1). On the covenantal reading, the door to God was not closed. It was moved. The new meeting place is Christ, and the new house is the people of God made of believing Jews and Gentiles (Ephesians 2:19-22). Scholars such as P. W. L. Walker note that Matthew never speaks of the judged temple being restored.
Acts 6:7: "a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith", even from the temple's own staff.
Romans 1:16: the gospel is God's power "to the Jew first and also to the Greek".

All Christian views agree that Jewish people are welcome in Christ now. Dispensationalists and many premillennialists add a future national restoration in the land with a central place for Jerusalem. Many amillennialists and postmillennialists expect a future large-scale conversion but not a return to temple worship.
What harm do failed end-time predictions do?
They damage trust in the Bible and in the church. People who were told the end would come on a date often conclude that prophecy itself is false.

Jesus began his answer with a warning: "See that no one leads you astray" (Matthew 24:4). On this reading, one modern form of being led astray is confident date-setting. A journalist once recalled reading, as a boy, an old book that said the world would end around 1934. He felt only relief that it was all past. Edgar Whisenant's book 88 Reasons said the rapture would come in September 1988. When it did not, he moved the date, then moved it to 1989. Each failure teaches outsiders that Christians cannot be trusted on the future. It also teaches believers to stop reading prophecy carefully. Scripture gives a test: a word that does not come to pass was not spoken by the Lord (Deuteronomy 18:21-22).
Edgar Whisenant's 88 Reasons Why the Rapture Will Be in 1988 sold millions of copies. The dates of September 11-13, 1988 passed without event.
In 1844 the Millerite movement expected Christ on October 22. The "Great Disappointment" left thousands disillusioned.

Most Christians of every view reject date-setting. Responsible futurists say no one can know the day (Matthew 24:36), but believers can still watch for signs that show the season is near (Matthew 24:33). They argue that false dates do not prove the signs are false, only that people misused them.
Is the world "stage set" for the end, as some modern writers have claimed?
This reading says such claims have been made in every age and keep failing. The signs Jesus gave belonged to his own generation, not to ours.

In 1988 John Walvoord wrote that the closing years of the twentieth century were pointing to end-time events. In his book on oil and the Middle East he said the world was like a stage set for a drama, with all actors ready. Television ministries announced that "the end of the world is coming soon". On the fulfilled reading, the problem is not watchfulness but misplaced signs. Jesus said the signs would come before his own generation passed (Matthew 24:34). Claims that "our generation" is the last have been made for centuries. Jack Van Impe once said the Soviet flag would fly over Independence Hall by 1976. Such sayings fade from memory, but they shape how people see the faith. Paul warned believers not to be quickly shaken by reports that the day had come (2 Thessalonians 2:2).
Medieval writers saw the year 1000, the Mongol invasions and the Black Death (1347-1351) as final signs.
Martin Luther believed the end was very near in the 1500s and that the Turks were Gog.

Futurists respond that Israel's return to the land in 1948, the growth of global systems and Middle East tensions are unique in history. They argue these fit Ezekiel 38 and Revelation 13 in a way earlier ages did not. Amillennial readers say the signs are present in every age between the comings.
Why does fulfilled prophecy strengthen faith?
Because it shows God knows and controls the future. Predictions made centuries before, and then fulfilled in detail, support the Bible's claim to be God's word.

God himself appeals to fulfilled prophecy: "I declare the end from the beginning" (Isaiah 46:9-10). Psalm 22 describes pierced hands and feet and the casting of lots for clothing. The Gospels show these happening at the cross (John 19:23-24). Isaiah 53 describes a servant who is wounded for others, silent before his accusers and buried with the rich. Isaiah wrote centuries before Jesus. Older writers counted hundreds of Old Testament predictions fulfilled in Christ. On the fulfilled reading, the New Testament's own prophecies should be expected to show the same accuracy. Jesus' words about the temple, the siege and the generation can be checked against history. When they are, the result strengthens faith. Speculation about tomorrow's headlines cannot do this, because it has not happened yet.
Micah 5:2 named Bethlehem as the Messiah's birthplace about seven centuries before Jesus was born there (Matthew 2:5-6).
Isaiah 44:28-45:1 names Cyrus as the one who would rebuild; Cyrus allowed the return in 538 BC (Ezra 1:1-4).

All Christian views value fulfilled prophecy. Futurists agree that many prophecies were fulfilled at the first coming. They say others, given in the same passages, wait for the second coming, as Isaiah 61:1-2 was split by Jesus in Luke 4:18-21. They see this as a model for a gap.
Was Jesus' prediction that no stone would be left on another fulfilled?
Yes. In AD 70 the Romans burned the temple and then pulled down its buildings. Josephus said visitors could hardly believe the place had been inhabited.

In August of AD 70 Roman soldiers set fire to the temple during the siege of Jerusalem. Josephus, a Jewish priest and historian who watched from the Roman camp, records that Titus then ordered the city and temple to be demolished. Only three towers and part of the western wall were left to show how strong the city had been (Jewish War 7.1.1). He wrote that nothing was left to make visitors believe the place had ever been lived in. Later Jewish tradition says a Roman officer ploughed the temple site, fulfilling Micah 3:12, "Zion shall be ploughed like a field" (Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 29a). Eusebius said he saw the site in ruins. On this reading, Jesus' word came true within about forty years, just as he said.
Josephus dates the burning to the tenth of the month Lous (Av), the same day Babylon had burned the first temple (Jewish War 6.4.5-8).
The Western Wall seen today belonged to the retaining wall of Herod's platform, not to the temple building Jesus pointed to.

Almost all interpreters accept this fulfillment. Some futurists point to the Western Wall and argue that a final, complete fulfillment awaits. Most scholars of all views answer that Jesus spoke of the temple buildings, which were completely destroyed, not the platform's outer support walls.
What did the disciples actually ask in Matthew 24:3?
They asked when the temple would fall, what sign would show Jesus' coming, and what would mark the end of the age. On this reading, all three concern one event.

The disciples asked: "When will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age?" The question came right after Jesus said the temple would be torn down. On the fulfilled reading, the parts are linked: (1) the time of the temple's ruin; (2) the sign of Jesus' coming in judgment connected with that ruin; (3) the end of the age that the temple's fall would bring. For a first-century Jew, the fall of the temple would mean the end of an era. Alfred Plummer noted that men who heard of the temple's overthrow would naturally think of it as the end of the age. Mark and Luke record the question only as "when will these things be, and what will be the sign?" (Mark 13:4; Luke 21:7). That suggests one event, not several far apart.
Mark 13:4: "Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?"
Luke 21:7 has the same simple form. Only Matthew adds "your coming" and "end of the age", for Jewish readers.

Many interpreters believe the disciples assumed the temple's fall and the end of the world would be one event. On this view, Jesus separated them in his answer: AD 70 first, then the final return after an unknown time. Dispensationalists often see the whole answer as future, with Luke 21:20-24 alone describing AD 70.
Did the disciples ask about the end of the "world" or the end of the "age"?
The Greek word is aion, "age", not kosmos, "world". This reading takes it as the end of the Old Covenant era, not the end of the planet.

The King James Version translates Matthew 24:3 as "the end of the world". But the Greek word is aion, which means an age or era. The word for the physical world is kosmos, which Matthew uses elsewhere (Matthew 24:21; 26:13). Most modern translations now read "end of the age". On this reading, the disciples were asking when time would run out for the temple, the city and the Mosaic system of sacrifices, washings and priests. Their focus was the building in front of them. Nothing in their training or in what Jesus had said would make them ask about the end of the physical universe. N. T. Wright makes this point: first-century Jews thought of the end of an era, not the end of space and time.
Matthew 13:39-40 uses the same phrase, "end of the age", in the parable of the weeds.
Hebrews 9:26 says Christ appeared "at the end of the ages" to put away sin, meaning his first coming.

All scholars agree the word means "age". Many say the age that ends is the present evil age before the age to come, which begins at the final return (Matthew 13:39-43; 28:20). On that view, "end of the age" still points to the last judgment, even if it is not the end of the physical world.
What were the "two ages" in Jewish thought, and how does that help here?
Jews spoke of "this age" and "the age to come", the age of the Messiah. This reading says the Messiah's arrival and the temple's fall marked the change between them.

Jewish teachers divided history into "this age" and "the age to come". The age to come was the time of the Messiah and of God's kingdom. Jesus used the same language (Matthew 12:32). The disciples asked before the ascension, "Will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" (Acts 1:6). They expected a change of age. On the fulfilled reading, the New Testament shows the change already underway. Paul says the ends of the ages had come upon his readers (1 Corinthians 10:11). Hebrews says believers have tasted "the powers of the age to come" (Hebrews 6:5). The old age, tied to the temple and the law, ended visibly when the temple fell. The Messiah's age had begun with his death, resurrection and enthronement.
George Hill, an 18th-century Scottish theologian, wrote that Jews divided time into the age of the law and the age of the Messiah.
Hebrews 8:13 (written before AD 70) says the old covenant is "becoming obsolete and growing old" and is "ready to vanish away".

Many scholars accept the two-age frame but say the ages overlap. The age to come has begun with Christ ("already") but will be complete only at his return ("not yet"). On this view, AD 70 was a key moment but not the full change. Dispensationalists see a future millennial age as well.
What exactly ended at "the end of the age" on this reading?
The Old Covenant system of temple, priests and animal sacrifice. Christ had replaced each part, and the temple's fall removed the last visible shadow.

On the covenantal reading, "end of the age" means the end of the Mosaic way of worship. Each part of it pointed to Christ. Jesus is the Lamb of God who takes away sin (John 1:29). He is the true temple where God dwells (John 2:19-21). He serves in the true tabernacle (Hebrews 8:2). He is the perfect high priest who offered himself once for all (Hebrews 7:26-27). The law was a guardian to lead us to Christ, and now that faith has come we are no longer under it (Galatians 3:24-25). The end of the age also meant the opening of the covenant to the Gentiles (Matthew 21:43; 22:9-10). When the temple fell, there was no place left to carry out the old system. The shadows had given way to the reality.
Romans 10:4 calls Christ "the end (telos) of the law" for righteousness to all who believe.
After AD 70 the daily sacrifice ceased. Jewish worship reshaped itself around prayer and study, led by the rabbis at Yavneh.

Most Christians agree Christ fulfilled the Old Covenant at the cross. Many date the end of the old order to the cross and resurrection rather than AD 70. Dispensationalists say the church age is a parenthesis and that God's program for national Israel, including a temple, resumes later.
What do Paul, Hebrews and Peter say about when the "end" was?
They speak of it as present or near: the ends of the ages "have come", Christ appeared "at the end of the ages", and "the end of all things is at hand".

Paul says the Old Testament stories were written "for our instruction, on whom the ends of the ages have come" (1 Corinthians 10:11). Hebrews says Christ "has appeared once for all at the end of the ages" (Hebrews 9:26). Peter says Christ was revealed "in these last times for your sake" (1 Peter 1:20). He also says "the end of all things is at hand" (1 Peter 4:7). James says "the coming of the Lord is at hand" (James 5:8). On the fulfilled reading, these writers understood that they were living in the final years of the old age. The end they expected was near to them. Milton Terry described it as the end of the pre-Messianic age, which Hebrews 12:26-27 pictures as a shaking of earth and heaven.
Hebrews 12:26-28: what can be shaken is removed so that the kingdom that cannot be shaken may remain.
2 Corinthians 3:13: Moses veiled his face so Israel would not see the end of what was "passing away".

Other readers say "last days" names the whole time between Christ's first and second comings. On this view, the nearness language expresses certainty and readiness, since a thousand years are like a day with the Lord (2 Peter 3:8). They argue the end has been "near" for the church in every age.
How can Jesus be said to have "come" in AD 70?
In the Old Testament God often "came" in judgment on nations without being seen. This reading says Jesus came in the same way, through the Roman armies.

The Old Testament often speaks of God "coming down" or "riding on a cloud" to judge. "The LORD is riding on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt" (Isaiah 19:1). That judgment came through the Assyrians. God "came down" to see Babel (Genesis 11:5). He came out of his place to tread on the high places of Samaria (Micah 1:3-6). In Psalm 18:9-14 David describes God coming on clouds with thunder to save him from Saul. No one saw God's body in these events. On the fulfilled reading, Jesus' coming in judgment on Jerusalem follows this pattern. Jesus said his generation would see these things (Matthew 24:34). So the "coming" of Matthew 24:27-30 must have a meaning that could be fulfilled then. It was a visible judgment showing that Jesus was enthroned.
Isaiah 19:1: "The LORD rides on a swift cloud" to Egypt. Assyria conquered Egypt in the 7th century BC.
Matthew 26:64: Jesus told the high priest, "You will see the Son of Man... coming on the clouds."

Futurists and most traditional readers hold that Matthew 24:30 describes the visible, bodily second coming (Acts 1:11). They accept God's "cloud comings" in the Old Testament but say the New Testament promises a personal return that every eye will see (Revelation 1:7). Partial preterists also expect that final return.
Do the warnings to the churches in Revelation 2-3 show that Jesus can "come" in a limited way?
Yes, on this reading. Jesus warned Ephesus, Pergamum and Sardis that he would "come" to them in judgment if they did not repent. That was not his final return.

Jesus told Ephesus, "I will come to you and remove your lampstand, unless you repent" (Revelation 2:5). He told Pergamum, "I will come to you soon and war against them with the sword of my mouth" (Revelation 2:16). He told Sardis, "I will come like a thief" (Revelation 3:3). These comings depend on whether a single church repents. They were threatened against a particular church at a particular time. So they cannot all be the one final return of Christ to the whole world. On the fulfilled reading, this shows the New Testament uses "coming" for acts of judgment in history. Jesus' coming against Jerusalem in AD 70 is the largest example. Robert Thomas has argued these are all forms of the second coming, but the conditional wording makes that hard.
